entry: Elimination of metabolic waste products by an [[Organism|organism]]. Excretion is essential in all organisms, because waste such as [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]], water, salts and [[Urea|urea]] is harmful if it accumulates beyond a certain level. In vertebrates, the main excretory organs are the [[Lung|lungs]], kidneys and skin. Unicellular organisms discharge wastes directly through the cell surface. In placental mammals, urine passes from the [[Bladder|bladder]] through the urethra, and solid waste leaves as [[Feces|feces]] during defecation. Birds excrete uric acid as a paste, which conserves water and can be stored in the egg, while in [[Insect|insects]] Malpighian tubules remove metabolic waste. Excretion differs from secretion, in which a substance has specific tasks after leaving the cell.

Method of [[Capital punishment|capital punishment]] in which several shooters fire simultaneously on command. Historically called fusillading, from the French *fusil*, meaning rifle, it was common in times of [[War|war]], because firearms are readily available and a gunshot to the [[Heart|heart]] usually kills relatively quickly. Simultaneous firing prevents identification of who fired the lethal shot. One or more shooters may be issued a blank cartridge, which is believed to diffuse responsibility among the squad.

Branch of government that executes and enforces law and policy. Its powers vary with the political context and are usually laid out in a [[Constitution|constitution]]. In democratic countries the executive often exercises broad influence over national politics, though limits are usually applied, and executives often rely on bureaucrats to formulate policy. In systems based on [[Separation of powers|separation of powers]], each branch is checked by the others: the executive or legislature can propose laws, the [[Legislature|legislature]] can pass or block them, the executive enforces them, and the [[Judiciary|judiciary]] interprets them. In parliamentary systems the executive is responsible to the elected legislature and must maintain its confidence, while in presidential systems the directly elected head of government appoints the ministers.

State of having being or reality, in contrast to nonexistence. Existence is often contrasted with essence, the essential features of an entity, which can be understood even when it is unknown whether the entity exists. [[Ontology|Ontology]] studies the nature and types of existence. Existence is usually treated as a second-order property, a property of properties, but some philosophers hold that it is a first-order property like color. Alexius Meinong and his followers say that not all individuals have it, so that [[Santa Claus|Santa Claus]] does not exist. Entities in space and time have concrete existence, unlike abstract entities such as [[Number|numbers]] and [[Set (mathematics)|sets]]. The concept has been discussed since ancient philosophy, including Presocratic philosophy in [[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greece]], and it is relevant to logic, mathematics, epistemology and the philosophy of mind.

Hypothesized risk to human existence from artificial superintelligence. Substantial progress toward superintelligence has been hypothesized to cause human extinction or another irreversible global catastrophe. Many researchers believe a superintelligent machine would resist attempts to disable it or change its goals. In May 2023, hundreds of AI experts signed a statement declaring that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority. In October 2025, hundreds of public figures called for a ban on developing superintelligence.

Family of philosophical views that explore the struggle to lead an authentic life despite the apparent absurdity of existence. Existentialist thought often examines meaning, purpose and value, and emphasizes personal freedom, individual responsibility and deliberate choice. Its 19th-century figures include [[Søren Kierkegaard|Søren Kierkegaard]], [[Friedrich Nietzsche|Friedrich Nietzsche]] and [[Fyodor Dostoevsky|Fyodor Dostoevsky]], who critiqued rationalism. In the mid-20th century it became associated with [[Jean-Paul Sartre|Jean-Paul Sartre]], [[Martin Heidegger|Martin Heidegger]], [[Simone de Beauvoir|Simone de Beauvoir]] and [[Albert Camus|Albert Camus]]. A primary virtue is authenticity, and Sartre argued that existence precedes essence. The movement influenced theology, drama, art, literature and psychology.

Planet outside the [[Solar System|Solar System]]. The first confirmed exoplanet was detected in 1992 around a [[Pulsar|pulsar]], and the first detection around a main-sequence star followed in 1995. As of November 5, 2026, there are 6,464 confirmed exoplanets in 4,849 planetary systems. Most have been found by transit photometry and Doppler [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopy]], methods biased toward large planets close to their stars. The nearest exoplanets orbit [[Proxima Centauri|Proxima Centauri]], 4.2 [[Light-year|light-years]] from Earth. Planets in a star's habitable zone, where liquid water could exist, are of special interest in the search for [[Extraterrestrial life|extraterrestrial life]], and the [[James Webb Space Telescope|James Webb Space Telescope]] is expected to reveal more about their composition.

Increase over time in distance between gravitationally unbound parts of the observable universe. The expansion is intrinsic, so it does not mean that the universe expands into anything. It is a key feature of [[Big Bang|Big Bang]] cosmology, modeled with [[General relativity|general relativity]], and was discovered through theoretical and observational work in the 1920s. Cosmic expansion decelerated until around 9.8 billion years after the Big Bang, when it began to accelerate gradually, a late-time effect attributed to [[Dark energy|dark energy]].

Average value of a [[Random variable|random variable]], generalizing the weighted average. For a variable with finitely many values, it is the weighted average of those values, with their probabilities as weights. Provided it is finite, it can be interpreted as the long-run average of results from independent repetitions of the same experiment, as formalized by the [[Law of large numbers|law of large numbers]]. The concept emerged in the mid-17th century from the problem of points, a puzzle about dividing stakes when a game ends early, which [[Blaise Pascal|Blaise Pascal]] and [[Pierre de Fermat|Pierre de Fermat]] solved independently. [[Christiaan Huygens|Christiaan Huygens]] published a treatise in 1657 that is seen as the first successful attempt to lay the foundations of probability theory.

Conscious event, especially perception, or the practical knowledge and familiarity that such events produce. In the widest sense, an experience presents a subject with various items, and unreal items may be included, as in [[Hallucination|hallucinations]] or dreams. In a narrower sense, experience is identified with sensory perception and contrasted with thinking or imagining. Experience can also mean familiarity gained through repeated acquaintance, as an experienced [[Hiking|hiker]] has lived through many hikes rather than merely read about them. [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|Phenomenology]] studies the structure and contents of experience, while [[Epistemology|epistemology]] asks whether all knowledge is based on sensory experience. Non-ordinary experiences include religious, out-of-body and near-death experiences.

Procedure carried out to support or refute a [[Hypothesis|hypothesis]], or to determine the efficacy or likelihood of something untried. Experiments provide insight into cause and effect by showing what outcome occurs when a particular factor is manipulated. They rely on a repeatable procedure and logical analysis of results, and range from informal comparisons, such as tasting chocolates to find a favorite, to highly controlled tests using complex apparatus. Experiments typically include controls, which minimize the effects of [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]] other than the single independent variable. Controls are part of the [[Scientific method|scientific method]]. In physics and engineering, experiments focus on replicating identical procedures, while in [[Medicine|medicine]] and the social sciences they often follow the form of the clinical trial, with units randomly assigned to treatment or control.

Process of investigating an unfamiliar area, an activity with some expectation of discovery. Organized exploration is largely a human activity, though exploratory behavior is common among organisms capable of directed locomotion and learning. Geographical exploration has had two major eras: the first, covering most of human history, saw peoples settle distant lands in relative isolation; the second, over the last 10,000 years, brought increased cross-cultural exchange. Between the 5th and 15th centuries AD, most exploration was done by Chinese and Arab explorers, and the [[Age of Discovery|Age of Discovery]] followed. The first modern [[Atlas|atlas]], by Abraham Ortelius, included a world map showing all of Earth's continents. Space exploration uses astronomy, which relies on [[Telescope|telescopes]], and space technology, including robotic probes and human spaceflight. Less than 10 percent of the ocean has been mapped in any detail.

Remote study of [[Mars|Mars]] by spacecraft, including orbiters, landers and rovers. Roughly 60 percent of spacecraft destined for Mars failed before completing their missions. [[Soviet space program|Soviet]] probes began the effort in 1960, and [[NASA|NASA]]'s Mariner 4 made the first successful flyby on July 14–15, 1965. Mars 3 achieved the first Martian soft landing in 1971. The [[Curiosity (rover)|Curiosity]] and Perseverance rovers, both operated by NASA, are on the surface, and six orbiters survey the planet. In April 2024, NASA selected several companies to begin studies on providing commercial services for robotic science on Mars.

Rapid expansion in volume of matter, associated with an extreme outward release of energy, usually with high temperatures and high-pressure gases. Supersonic explosions created by high explosives are detonations, which travel as shock waves, while subsonic explosions by low explosives proceed by slower combustion known as deflagration. Explosive volcanic eruptions occur when dissolved gas in rising [[Magma|magma]] bubbles out of solution, causing a rapid increase in volume. Astronomical explosions include [[Supernova|supernovae]] and impacts such as the [[Tunguska event|Tunguska event]] of 1908, believed to have resulted from a meteor air burst. Gunpowder was the first explosive to be invented, and [[Alfred Nobel|Alfred Nobel]] invented [[Dynamite|dynamite]] in 1866. Humans also create explosions through explosives or through nuclear fission or fusion, as in a [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapon]].

Probability distribution of the distance between events in a Poisson point process, in which events occur independently at a constant average rate. It is a particular case of the [[Gamma distribution|gamma distribution]] and the continuous analogue of the [[Geometric distribution|geometric distribution]]. Its probability density function is f(x) = λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0, where the rate parameter λ is greater than 0. The mean is 1/λ, the [[Variance|variance]] is 1/λ², and the standard deviation equals the mean. The [[Median|median]] is ln(2)/λ, which is less than the [[Expected value|expected value]]. The distribution is memoryless: the remaining waiting time has the same distribution whatever time has already passed.

Mathematical function, usually written e^x or exp(x), that maps zero to one. It is the unique real function that equals its own [[Derivative|derivative]] and takes the value one at zero. It converts sums to products, exp(x+y) = exp(x)·exp(y), and its inverse is the [[Natural logarithm|natural logarithm]]. It is the sum of the power series whose terms are x^n/n!, which converges for every real number. Functions of the form b^x with a fixed base b are also called exponential functions, and they grow or decay exponentially. [[Euler's formula|Euler's formula]] extends the function to [[Complex number|complex numbers]], relating multiplication, rotation and trigonometry.

Modernist movement, initially in poetry and painting, that presents the world solely from a subjective perspective. It originated in Northern Europe around the beginning of the 20th century, distorting the world radically for emotional effect rather than depicting physical reality. Expressionism developed as an [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] style before the First World War and remained popular in [[Berlin|Berlin]] during the Weimar Republic. It extended to architecture, theatre, dance, film and music, and was partly a reaction to [[Impressionism|Impressionism]]. In Germany, Die Brücke, formed in [[Dresden|Dresden]] in 1905, and Der Blaue Reiter, formed in [[Munich|Munich]] in 1911 with [[Wassily Kandinsky|Wassily Kandinsky]], were key groups. The movement declined in Germany with the rise of [[Adolf Hitler|Adolf Hitler]] in the 1930s.

Family that extends beyond the [[Nuclear family|nuclear family]] to include aunts, uncles, grandparents, cousins and other relatives, living nearby or in the same household. A stem family, first discussed by Frédéric Le Play, has parents living with one child, that child's spouse and their children, while other children leave or remain unmarried. Stem families are associated with unequal inheritance in [[Japan|Japan]] and [[Korea|Korea]], while in traditional [[Romania|Romania]] and northeastern [[Thailand|Thailand]] the child who cares for the parents usually receives the house. Extended families often form support networks even when living apart, and [[Facebook|Facebook]] is commonly used to maintain these ties. An estimated 49 million Americans, or 16.1 percent of the total population, live in homes with three or more generations, up from 42 million in 2000.

Theoretical extension of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]] to chemical elements beyond those known and proven. The heaviest known element is [[Oganesson|oganesson]], atomic number 118, which completes the seventh period. Further periods are expected to add a g-block of at least 18 elements, as in an eight-period table suggested by Glenn T. Seaborg in 1969. Relativistic models predict that the pattern will be broken for heavier elements. Element 126 is hypothesized to lie within an [[Island of stability|island of stability]] that resists fission but not alpha decay.

Absorption and scattering of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] by dust and gas between an astronomical object and the observer. Interstellar extinction was first documented as such in 1930 by Robert Julius Trumpler, though its effects on the colors of stars had been noted earlier. Because blue light is attenuated more strongly than red, extinction makes objects appear redder, a phenomenon called interstellar reddening. Interstellar reddening differs from redshift, which shifts spectra without distortion. Near the plane of the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]], visual extinction is roughly 1.8 magnitudes per kiloparsec. Strong atmospheric extinction in the X-ray, ultraviolet and infrared is overcome by space-based observatories.

Widespread and rapid decrease in biodiversity on Earth, also called a mass extinction or biotic crisis. It is identified by a sharp fall in the diversity and abundance of multicellular organisms. Estimates of major mass extinctions in the last 540 million years range from five to more than twenty. During the [[Phanerozoic|Phanerozoic]], multicellular animal life has experienced at least five major mass extinctions. The [[Late Ordovician mass extinction|Late Ordovician mass extinction]] killed 85 percent of all species, and the [[Late Devonian mass extinction|Late Devonian]] extinctions were linked to anoxic events in which seawater was deprived of oxygen. Volcanism at the [[Siberian Traps|Siberian Traps]] is linked to the end-[[Permian|Permian]] extinction.

Life originating on a world other than Earth, also called alien life. No extraterrestrial life has yet been detected. Speculation about inhabited worlds dates back to antiquity, and since the mid-20th century researchers have searched for life and intelligence, including the 1960 Project Ozma experiment and NASA's Viking program on [[Mars|Mars]]. Thought experiments such as the [[Drake equation|Drake equation]] estimate the probability of intelligent life elsewhere, and current solar system studies focus on Venus, Mars, [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] and [[Titan (moon)|Titan]]. Interstellar travel remains largely hypothetical, although [[Voyager 1|Voyager 1]] and [[Voyager 2|Voyager 2]] have entered the interstellar medium. The subject has strongly influenced science fiction.

Large-scale low-pressure system of the middle latitudes, also called a mid-latitude or wave cyclone. Extratropical cyclones generally form between 30 and 60 degrees of [[Latitude|latitude]] and, with anticyclones, drive much of the weather in those regions. They can produce everything from wind and mild showers to severe [[Hail|hail]], thunderstorms, [[Blizzard|blizzards]] and [[Tornado|tornadoes]]. Unlike [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]], they produce rapid changes in temperature and dew point along broad [[Weather front|weather fronts]]. They form along zones of temperature and dew-point gradient, where upper-level divergence beneath a [[Jet stream|jet stream]] lowers surface pressure. They are classified as baroclinic, and later in their life cycle the cyclone occludes and weakens.

Central dimension of human personality, introduced into psychology by [[Carl Jung|Carl Jung]]. Extraversion is associated with sociability, talkativeness and high energy, while introversion is linked to [[Introspection|introspection]], reserve and a preference for solitary activities. Jung defined introversion as an orientation through subjective psychic contents, and extraversion as a concentration of interest on the external object. These traits are measured in degrees rather than fixed categories. Although often presented as opposite ends of a continuum, most people have elements of both, with one more dominant depending on the situation.

Activity, also called an action sport, perceived as involving a high degree of risk of injury or death. Extreme sports often involve speed, height, high physical exertion and specialized gear, and are affected by uncontrollable variables such as wind, snow, water and mountains. The term gained popularity in the 1990s, when marketers used it to promote the X Games and the Extreme Sports Channel. [[Skateboarding|Skateboarding]], [[Snowboarding|snowboarding]], [[Surfing|surfing]] and [[Climbing|climbing]] are examples. Judging is often subjective and aesthetic rather than unified. Bungee jumping was pioneered by members of the Dangerous Sports Club of Oxford University, who made the first modern jumps on April 1, 1979, from the Clifton Suspension Bridge in Bristol, England.
